Subject: Re: Broken OO-parent-method call & can()

Yitzchak Scott-Thoennes wrote:
> On Fri, October 26, 2007 12:05 pm, Linda W wrote:
>> Rafael Garcia-Suarez wrote:
>>
>>> Linda W wrote:
>>>
>>>> I'm firmly of the opinion that "\\&foo" should return "undef" at
>>>> execution time if \\&foo is not defined (i.e. &foo doesn't exist).
>>> A function can exist, but be undefined :
>>> $ perl -wle 'sub foo;print defined &foo print exists &foo'
>>> 1
----
	I disagree with my former self.  I won't say I firmly
am of opinion that \\&foo should return undef at execution time as it would
not be consistent with other var access.
	This doesn't mean I don't want a chance reference to a non-existent
local routine " {\\&nonlocalsub }, interfering with a call through a blessed
reference.

> 
> The dispatch table in BEGIN block (http://perlmonks.org/?node_id=647782)
> example in your perlmonks thread (http://perlmonks.org/?node_id=647749)
> provides an IMO unarguable, if rare, use case
---
	I'm not arguing for use of that dispatch table -- but I am arguing
that a "stray", "random" reference to an undefined sub should *OVERRIDE*
an OO-call properly looking up the method.

	The jump table you mention originally referred to all package
local calls, making all of the entries valid.  It was when the handling
routines got split into separate packages (classes) that the jump-table
no longer functioned.  I'm not arguing that the jump table, across packages
or classes "should" work.  Makes sense that it doesn't.

> .  (And \\ returning undef in
> general seems very wrong to me.)  So \\&foo really needs to create a forward
> declaration.
---
	That's fine...I "think" I agree...:-)
> And because forward declarations must affect method resolution

> (see example in http://perlmonks.org/?node_id=647781), we're pretty much
> stuck with things as they are.
----
	Just because correctly functioning code is "hard" or
'difficult" doesn't mean it should be avoided. A *defined* forward
reference should affect method resolution, but in OO implementation,
before OO returns a "method is undefined" error, it should look
through the parent classes.

> (The only possible "fix" I see would be making \\&, when it creates a
> forward declaration, set a special flag saying to ignore that CV when doing
> method resolution, making it have a special "semi-exists" state.  But
> the idea of that makes me ill.)
---
	But when a function is "forward referenced", but not defined,
it already is in a "semi-exists" state.  I'm saying that when a function
is in that "quasi" state, it shouldn't *override* the parental lookup
machinery.  This was the *bug* I brought to the table  on 9-29.  That's
a MONTH ago.  Nobody had a clue that local, undefined methods would
stop perl's OO lookup machinery from working.

	On the other hand -- I strongly suspect I am not the only one
who has encounter this.  I'm just the first person who decided not to work
around the buggy code like everyone else does (don't use references;
use strings for method calls).  That sounded "superstitious" to me.  I
wanted to know what was wrong with what I was doing -- not just code
around it.

	When I did find the bug, it was big enough to drive a truck
through.  Many people suggested ways to work around this bug, but when
I pushed back with examples of things that didn't work -- that should have,
those people just stopped responding -- they had more important things
to do than going on some perl-bug hunt.  They knew how to work around
it -- that was the "accepted" way to do things (because taking the
reference would activate the bug), so why waste time tracking down why
my code was "broken".

	The above behavior -- where experienced perl-coders knew
"instinctively", the way to work around it indicates to me that while
all of them knew how to code around that "buggy area", none of them were
able to tell me what part of my code was "incorrect" or why.

> So this seems very much a DDTT situation.  
---
	DDTT? (Don't do that thing?)  Regardless -- because
of people reactions to my probing (for a month), I don't think the
case is as infrequent as you would like to believe.  It's just
no one has been willing to deal with the flack "you don't know what
you are doing" or "you just aren't willing to take our help" (i.e.
not willing to code "differently", while not understanding why).

	Regardless of my reasons for pursuing the problem, when
the function is "defined by reference" and not really defined, it
is in a "quasi" state.  Why can't it look through the parent's methods
before throwing a fatal error?  It's not like it is going to be a
performance sensitive case, since the alternative if it isn't fixed
is just to die with a fatal error.
